description: Presentations on Cryptography at DEF CON 23 covers secure messaging protocols, applied cryptographic primitives, cryptocurrency brainwallet cracking, and SSL/TLS time synchronization bypasses.

talks.title: Secure Messaging for Normal People
talks.teaser: Justin Engler examines end-to-end encryption usability, key management, and cryptographic challenges in building secure messaging systems for mainstream users.
talks.summary:
The Usability Crisis in End-to-End Encryption

Justin Cappos and colleagues analyze why robust cryptographic protocols historically failed to achieve widespread consumer adoption. While end-to-end encryption algorithms like RSA, AES, and Diffie-Hellman are mathematically sound, complex user experiences, key management burdens, and opaque security indicators alienate non-technical users.

Modern Ratchet Protocols and Forward Secrecy

The speakers evaluate modern cryptographic protocols, particularly the Signal protocol (Double Ratchet), which automate session key renewal and provide forward secrecy and post-compromise security without requiring manual user intervention. Transparent key exchange allows applications to secure messaging while retaining the intuitive simplicity of standard SMS.

Preventing Man-in-the-Middle Attacks Usably

A major focus is human verification of cryptographic identities. The presentation evaluates alternative identity confirmation mechanisms, comparing hexadecimal fingerprint comparison against QR code scanning, short authentication strings (SAS), and automated safety number change notifications across popular messaging platforms.

Architectural Trade-offs for Mass Adoption

Balancing metadata privacy, multi-device synchronization, and offline message storage introduces complex engineering trade-offs. The authors conclude that cryptographic security must be integrated as an invisible, default primitive rather than an opt-in feature to protect vulnerable populations effectively.

talks.title: Alice and Bob are Really Confused
talks.teaser: David Huerta explores the human factors and usability failures of cryptographic tools, demonstrating how poor UX undermines real-world privacy and key management.
talks.summary:
User Experience Failures in Operational Cryptography

David Huerta examines the persistent disconnect between cryptographic tool design and the mental models of everyday users, activists, and journalists. Traditional operational security software often relies on hostile user interfaces, confusing terminology, and counterintuitive key management workflows that actively induce dangerous user errors.

Deconstructing the PGP Key Lifecycle

Huerta dissects the usability pitfalls inherent in the OpenPGP/GPG ecosystem, from key generation and subkey configuration to public key server distribution and web-of-trust validation. The cognitive overhead required to maintain and verify keys correctly causes even experienced security practitioners to make catastrophic operational mistakes.

Human-Centered Security Design Principles

The presentation demonstrates how security software can incorporate modern human-computer interaction (HCI) methodologies. By prioritizing empathetic UX design, eliminating cryptographic jargon, and providing clear, actionable warnings during security-critical decisions, developers can build tools that encourage safe behavior.

Fostering Accessible Privacy Tools

Huerta argues that security and privacy should be universal rights accessible to all users, not privileges reserved for technical elites. Designing accessible cryptographic interfaces requires continuous user testing with non-technical audiences, empathetic threat modeling, and moving past elitist assumptions in the hacker community.

talks.title: Breaking SSL Using Time Synchronisation Attacks
talks.teaser: Jose Selvi demonstrates how manipulating Network Time Protocol (NTP) synchronisation allows bypassing SSL/TLS certificate expiration checks and HSTS protections.
talks.summary:
The Dependency of Security Protocols on System Time

Jose Selvi explores how operating systems, web browsers, and cryptographic protocols rely fundamentally on accurate local clocks. Core security mechanisms—including SSL/TLS certificate validation, HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS), Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs), and automated software update routines—depend entirely on temporal bounds.

Insecurities in Network Time Synchronization

Selvi demonstrates that most consumer and enterprise operating systems synchronize time over unauthenticated Network Time Protocol (NTP) streams. Attackers in a position to intercept network traffic (such as rogue Wi-Fi access points or compromised local gateways) can spoof NTP responses to manipulate a target system's clock arbitrarily.

Exploiting Time Skew to Bypass TLS and HSTS

By forcing a machine's clock forward or backward, an attacker can bypass critical transport security protections. Selvi shows how advancing time past an HSTS policy expiration enables SSL-stripping attacks, while rewinding the clock allows attackers to present expired SSL certificates or exploit revoked credentials without triggering browser warnings.

Manipulating Windows Updates and Defensive Mitigations

The presentation demonstrates time synchronization exploitation against Windows Update, showing how forced time shifts can disrupt patch validation and update scheduling. Defending against NTP manipulation requires implementing authenticated time protocols (NTPsec), enforcing multi-source consensus algorithms, and sanity-checking drastic clock jumps within operating system kernels.
